title: 'Silence' — Technical Schematic and Field Reference
body:
# 'Silence' — Technical Schematic and Field Reference
## Constructed by Dae-jung Seo — One of a Kind

---

## PART ONE: THE BLADE — FROM TIP TO TANG

A katana is a laminated weapon. It is not one piece of steel but two bonded layers, each with a different material and a different job, built around a structure that Japanese swordsmiths refined over centuries and that Torii's Advanced Weapons Division adapted for 23rd-century function. What follows describes every named part of the TSK-4, from the tip of the blade to the end of the handle.

**Kissaki** (the tip): The pointed end of the blade. On a traditional katana the kissaki has a distinct curved geometry — a small triangular section set off by the yokote line. On the TSK-4 the kissaki maintains this geometry. It is the most structurally vulnerable part of the blade — the nanotube composite kawagane is thinner here, and the shingane core tapers. Kyle does not use the tip for thrusting; the carbon-nanotube edge is maintained for slashing geometry, and a thrust into bone risks fracture propagation in the kissaki. He uses the tip for placement — precise contact to interface points.

**Yokote** (the tip boundary line): The line running perpendicular to the blade that marks where the kissaki ends and the ji begins. On the TSK-4 it is visible as a faint geometric transition in the kawagane surface. It marks where the kissaki geometry changes.

**Ji** (the flat): The broad flat of the blade between the hamon line and the mune. The largest visible surface area of the blade. On the TSK-4 the ji is matte black — light-absorbing carbon-nanotube kawagane, non-reflective, with no visible grain. In low light the blade effectively disappears against dark backgrounds. The hamon line runs across the ji's lower boundary and is the only light source on the blade surface.

**Hamon** (the temper line — the charge gauge): The line running lengthwise along the blade between the hardened edge steel and the softer spine steel. On a traditional blade this is a consequence of differential heat treatment. On the TSK-4 it is that, and also a real-time charge indicator: the hamon is doped with electroluminescent compounds driven directly by the supercapacitor voltage state. At zero charge the line glows cold blue, barely visible in daylight. As charge accumulates it brightens through cyan and white-blue to sodium-white at full capacity. In darkness at full charge, the hamon casts enough light to read by. The emission is passive and direct — it cannot be remotely triggered, cannot be electronically spoofed, and cannot fail independent of the supercapacitor bank itself. If the hamon is bright, the blade is charged.

**Ha** (the edge): The cutting side of the blade. The single sharpened edge runs from kissaki to hamachi (the notch at the base of the blade where the edge meets the guard). On the TSK-4 the ha is carbon-nanotube composite maintained at molecular-level geometry — a single row of aligned nanotubes along the cutting boundary, each a hollow cylinder roughly one nanometer across. The edge does not dull. It chips. Kyle checks it every morning: three fingers along the flat, feeling for micro-fractures. When it chips the fractures propagate along the nanotube grain; left unrepaired the blade eventually shatters. Embedded in the kawagane along the ha side is the passive neural disruption layer — a piezoelectric matrix separate from the shingane's harvesting system. On contact with any electrically-charged augmentation, this layer generates a localized electromagnetic pulse that cascades through the connected system. The implant crashes. No stored charge required. Always active.

**Shinogi** (the ridge line): The raised longitudinal ridge running along the blade between the ji and the mune. This geometry is structural — it stiffens the blade against lateral flex while keeping overall mass low. The shinogi is slightly more pronounced on the TSK-4 than on traditional blades because the PZT shingane core is heavier than iron at equivalent dimensions, shifting the blade's internal mass distribution. The shinogi compensates by providing additional bending resistance. It is also the boundary line along which the TENG film terminates — the triboelectric surface covers the mune face from shinogi to spine, not the ji.

**Mune** (the spine / the back): The thick, rounded back of the blade opposite the ha. In traditional construction the mune is soft iron, left unsharpened. On the TSK-4 the mune surface carries two energy systems. A TENG (triboelectric nanogenerator) film sits over a ferrocerium-titanium pyrophoric alloy substrate. When the mune drags against any surface harder than approximately 3 Mohs — concrete, asphalt, steel, rebar, vehicle panels — two things happen simultaneously. The TENG film generates electrical charge through triboelectric contact separation: electron transfer between the PTFE film surface and the counterpart material, harvested by a patterned aluminum electrode grid embedded in the film. And the ferrocerium substrate produces pyrophoric sparks: particles of the mischmetal alloy, stripped by abrasion, oxidizing instantly at 900 to 1400 degrees Celsius on contact with air. These sparks are real heat. The drag leaves real marks on every surface. The sound is a bone-resonant screech. The mune is the charging face — the loud face, the aggressive face, the face that interacts with the environment rather than the target.

The critical limitation: triboelectric generation requires dry contact. Water between the TENG surface and a counterpart material bleeds charge before collection. In ambient humidity above 70%, TENG output drops 60 to 80 percent. In active rain it approaches zero. The pyrophoric sparks are unaffected — fire does not care about rain — but without the TENG film harvesting, drag does not accumulate charge. In GLMZ's wet Great Lakes climate this is the defining tactical constraint of the drag system.

**Kawagane** (the outer shell): The hard outer layer of the laminate that wraps the shingane inner core and forms all visible blade surfaces — the ji, the ha, the shinogi, and part of the mune. On the TSK-4 this is aligned carbon-nanotube composite: a material with no analog in traditional swordsmithing, giving the blade its absolute matte-black appearance and its molecular-level edge geometry. The kawagane is harder than any natural steel, lighter than iron at equivalent thickness, and the source of the blade's passive neural disruption capability through the embedded piezoelectric matrix on the ha side.

**Shingane** (the inner core): The inner core running the full length of the blade from nakago to kissaki, wrapped inside the kawagane. In traditional blades this is soft iron that absorbs shock and prevents brittle fracture. On the TSK-4 it is PZT-5H ceramic plates bonded in a T700 carbon-fiber matrix. PZT (lead zirconate titanate) is a piezoelectric material: it generates voltage when mechanically stressed. Every impact load delivered to the blade — a clash against another weapon, a hard surface strike, a caught parry — compresses and shears the PZT plates and generates electrical charge. The carbon-fiber matrix prevents catastrophic fracture of the brittle ceramic under tension while allowing the compressive and shear stresses from impact to couple efficiently into the PZT lattice. The charge scales with the square of the impact force: a full-force power parry generates 15 to 40 times the charge of a glancing deflection at the same apparent speed. Kinetic energy is one-half mass times velocity squared, and this means the blade rewards aggression disproportionately. A fighter who stands in and takes hard parries charges the system far faster than one who deflects and angles away.

The acoustic consequence: piezoelectric elements convert mechanical resonance to charge continuously until the resonance decays. When two blades clash and the blade rings, the shingane is still generating charge throughout the decay of that ring. A loud, clean, high-pitched ring after a hard parry means the core is still feeding. A dull thud means almost nothing was harvested. The hamon brightens perceptibly during the oscillation period. The ring after a hard parry is diagnostic: a loud, clean, sustained tone means the core fed well. A dull thud means almost nothing was harvested. Replacing the shingane requires a qualified bladesmith and 4 to 8 hours with the blade out of service. This is not a field repair.

**Nakago** (the tang): The portion of the blade that extends into and is hidden inside the handle. The nakago carries electrode leads from both harvesting systems — the TENG film on the mune and the PZT shingane core — routed through channels to the supercapacitor bank in the tsuka. It also carries the hardware interface for the field-swappable tsuka connection. The TSK-4 serial number is laser-etched on the inner curve of the tsuba at the nakago entry point, visible only on disassembly.

**Tsuba** (the guard): The flat oval disc between the blade and the handle that protects the hand. On the TSK-4 it is tungsten carbide — no ornamentation, no engraving on the external faces, completely unadorned. Flat, oval, matte-grey. Kyle has replaced the cord wrap around the tsuba joint twice. The tungsten carbide disc itself has never needed replacement.

**Tsuka** (the handle): The grip section of the sword, wrapped in tsukaito cord. Under the cord wrapping is a graphene ultracapacitor bank using ionic liquid electrolyte — the highest energy density supercapacitor chemistry achievable in the tsuka's available volume, approximately 15 to 20 cubic centimeters once the nakago channel and structural material are accounted for. Rated storage: approximately 200 millijoules. Both harvesting systems route their output through electrode leads in the nakago to this bank.

The tsuka is field-swappable. It slides off the nakago in under two minutes and can be replaced with a pre-charged spare — Kyle carries one spare in the same way a shooter carries a spare magazine. The tsukaito wrapping shows a faint luminescence through the cord when the bank is significantly charged. Subtle in ambient light, visible in darkness.

For context on the 200 millijoule capacity: a standard Taser delivers 50 to 150 millijoules to a target. 200 millijoules delivered in under a millisecond to a cyberware interface point is sufficient to overwhelm surge protection on any commercial or civilian-grade augmentation. Military-hardened augmentation with shielded bus architecture requires either multiple discharges or a strike to an unshielded connection point.

---

## PART TWO: THE TWO FACES — HA AND MUNE

The katana is a single-edge blade. This is the design fact that makes the TSK-4's energy systems possible without interference between them.

The mune and the ha are on opposite faces of the blade. When the mune is dragging against a concrete floor throwing sparks and charging the supercapacitor, the ha is pointing away from any surface — not wasting its disruption capability on empty air, not dulling on anything. When the ha is in contact with a target, the mune is on the opposite side of the blade, untouched. The two systems cannot interfere with each other because they are physically separated.

The mune charges the battery. The ha uses the battery. They do not compete.

---

## PART THREE: CHARGE AND DISCHARGE

**Charging — drag (mune):** Drag the mune against any surface harder than 3 Mohs. The TENG film generates charge. The ferrocerium produces sparks. Three to five seconds of drag on dry concrete at pressure brings the hamon from cold to perceptibly lit. Ten meters of full-pressure drag on dry concrete produces 0.8 to 1.4 millijoules. In rain, TENG output approaches zero — fall back to clash-charging entirely.

**Charging — clash (shingane):** Every significant blade impact generates charge through the PZT core. A full-force parry against a heavy weapon generates 2 to 25 microcoulombs depending on impact force. The ring after impact continues charging until it fades. Works in any weather.

**Precharging — draw strop:** Kyle wears a corundum (Al2O3, Mohs 9) ceramic bracer on his inner left forearm. On the draw stroke, the mune crosses the bracer surface. Corundum abrades the ferrocerium substrate and is triboelectrically positive against the TENG film's PTFE layer, maximizing charge separation. Three to four deliberate passes before an engagement provides meaningful precharge. The gesture reads as a corrupted chiburi — the post-cut blade-cleaning motion — performed in reverse.

**Passive discharge (always available, no charge required):** The ha contacts any electrically-charged augmentation. The passive neural disruption layer generates a localized cascade that shorts the contacted system and everything connected to it. No stored charge consumed. Always on.

**Active discharge (requires accumulated charge):** The supercapacitor bank drains through the contact point in a single pulse. The passive mode cuts a wire. The active discharge blows the fuse box — all connected augmentation shorts simultaneously, amplified by the stored charge. After discharge: hamon resets to cold blue, bank empty, fight continues on passive only.

---

## PART FOUR: THE CARDIAC INTERFACE — STOP AND START

The TSK-4 can stop an augmented heart and start one. These are not the same mechanism.

**Stopping:** The ha's passive disruption layer, applied precisely to a cardiac regulator interface point, crashes the regulator firmware. Heart stops. No stored charge required. Requires that the target has a cardiac implant and that Kyle has identified the interface location via Augmentation Signature Read. Common cardiac regulator interface locations: the left lateral throat (most Tier 2 through 4 civilian implants), behind the sternum, and the left wrist underside (Torii Military Division units).

**Starting:** A crashed cardiac regulator has halted firmware, not a damaged heart. 200 millijoules delivered through the interface point reboots the firmware, which resumes cardiac pacing. The heart restarts. This is not classical defibrillation — classical defibrillation delivers 120 to 360 joules to reset disorganized electrical activity in the heart muscle itself. The TSK-4's 200 millijoules cannot do this. What it can do is reboot firmware. Silence can restart someone whose heart stopped because their implant crashed. It cannot restart someone whose heart stopped from physical damage or infarction. After restart discharge: hamon goes cold, bank empty.

**Kyle's own heart — False Death Protocol:** Kyle's cardiac regulator runs custom firmware with a 240-second restart delay. A specific NeoCortex signal crashes his own regulator — heart stops, countdown begins. His Cerebral Oxygenation Assist (installed by the NeoCortex program, never removed) maintains minimal brain perfusion for the duration. He presents as clinically dead. Vital-sign scanners read confirmed death. At T+240 seconds the regulator restarts and the heart resumes. The Cerebral Oxygenation Assist has 8 minutes of reserve. The protocol runs 4. That margin is not comfortable. The cardiac regulator interface at Kyle's left lateral throat is accessible to Silence's passive disruption mode. He wears his collar up.

---

## PART FIVE: OPERATIONAL SUMMARY

The blade has two modes and one constant.

The constant is the passive neural disruption layer on the ha — always on, always free, shorting anything chrome that the edge touches.

Quiet mode: A single precise cut to an augmented target's interface point. The chrome goes silent. The target is alive but stripped of augmentation. Seo's preferred technique was the wrist — eliminate the draw without killing. Kyle uses this when the contract says alive.

Loud mode: Drag the mune on any available surface. Let the sparks run. Accumulate charge through hard parries — stand in, take the hit clean, let the blade ring. Watch the hamon. When it goes sodium-white, the next contact delivers an active discharge: every piece of chrome the target carries fails simultaneously.

Weather shapes the choice. In covered spaces the mune charges rapidly on drag. In rain the drag is theater — TENG output is near zero, and the blade charges slowly through clash only. GLMZ is a wet city. Kyle prefers covered spaces and positions himself there before the fight starts when he can.

He maintains the blade before he maintains himself. The blade maintains him in return. They have an arrangement.

---

*Document compiled from Torii Security Group Advanced Weapons Division manufacturing specifications (recovered), Cascades Energy Systems component datasheets (partial), and field observation of TSK-4 in active use.*
